title: refactor(ci): unify lint/test/release workflows and optimize cache/parallelism
author: Marissa Cole
release_notes: Consolidate CI workflows: unify lint/test/release pipelines, introduce composite actions to reduce duplication, improve cache keys and parallelism settings to reduce overall CI time. No runtime behavior changes to product code.
description:
Context: Over the last year the GH Actions workflows for lint, unit/integration tests, and release automation have diverged and accumulated duplication. This increases maintenance cost and leads to inconsistent cache usage and slower runs. This PR consolidates common steps into reusable composite actions, unifies the lint/test/release workflows into a smaller set of well-documented jobs, and tunes cache keys + matrix/parallelism to improve throughput and cache hit rate.

What changed: consolidated .github/workflows/{lint.yml,test.yml,release.yml} into a unified set of workflow templates and composite actions under .github/actions/ci-helpers. Added a cache-utils script to standardize keys across Node and Python jobs; introduced a small top-level matrix for test jobs with smarter parallelism bounds; reduced duplicated steps (checkout/setup, restore/cache, setup-node/python, install) by moving them to reusable composites. Kept release job logic intact but moved tagging and changelog steps into a composite for reuse.

Checklist: - [x] Move common steps into composite actions and templates; - [x] Standardize cache key naming for node_modules/venv and tool caches; - [x] Add CI metrics logs (step durations) for the first 2 weeks; - [x] Run full CI on main and on a release candidate branch; - [x] Add rollback notes and revert plan.

Testing: Ran full matrix on feature branch; observed median reduction in total CI runtime for pull requests (~18-25% depending on job mix). Re-ran flaky integration tests that previously caused intermittent failures and adjusted test grouping for better parallel throughput. Verified release workflow still creates draft releases and tags correctly on a dry-run on release-candidate branch.

Why this is safe: No production code changes. All changes are CI-only and documented. Composite actions are backwards-compatible; old workflows are removed only after successful runs observed for a week. If regressions in caching or job orchestration are detected we can revert the composite actions directory and re-enable the previous workflows (revert instructions added at the top of the README).

Notes for reviewers: focus on cache key correctness, permission scopes for composite actions, and any org-level constraints for reusable actions. I left a short migration guide in .github/actions/README.md.
